lesson.title: Greetings & Goodbyes Gym
lesson.subtitle: Guten Tag, Hallo, Tschüss, Auf Wiedersehen — dialogue drills with the du/Sie switch

hook.title: The Social Scripts
hook.content: Greetings are whole sentences wearing costumes. Guten Tag = 'good day'. Auf Wiedersehen = 'until re-seeing' — a farewell that promises a next time. Tschüss = the sailor's Tschüss, bent from French adieu. Hallo is your own hello, borrowed back. And the dialogue runs on the dative you already own: Wie geht's? — Danke, gut! — Und Ihnen? (formal) / Und dir? (informal). Today you drill the scripts until the switch between formal and informal is automatic — because that switch is the first social test every German conversation gives you.

footnotes.title: Moin, the North's Universal
footnotes.content: Northern Germany answers with Moin — morning, day, evening, it works around the clock. Etymologically unrelated to Morgen: it may come from Low German mooi ('nice'). One syllable, zero conjugation, total coverage.

pattern.title: The Scripts, Formal and Informal
pattern.content: Formal script: Guten Tag! — Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen? — Danke, gut, und Ihnen? — Auf Wiedersehen! Informal script: Hallo! / Morgen! — Wie geht's? — Danke, gut! Und dir? — Tschüss! / Bis bald! The pieces: Guten Morgen (before noon), Guten Abend (evening), Gute Nacht (bedtime — the ghost-map word!). The verbs: sehen (see — Wiedersehen), gehen (geht in wie geht's). Notice the case: Guten Tag is masculine ACCUSATIVE — 'I wish [you a] good day', the wish-object — and Gute Nacht is feminine: the article reports the gender of the noun.
pattern.linguist_note: Auf Wiedersehen parses as auf (until/on) + wieder (again) + sehen (see) — and wieder itself hides the Germanic *wiþrō, the same root as English 'with' in its original 'against/return' sense. The goodbye is a small etymology sandwich.

exercises.prompt: Match each greeting with its literal reading:
exercises.target_answer: Guten Tag, Auf Wiedersehen, Guten Abend, Gute Nacht
exercises.meaning: hello, formal goodbye, good evening, good night
exercises.explanation: Guten Tag wishes a good day (masculine accusative); Gute Nacht is feminine — the article reports the noun's gender.

exercises.prompt: You are leaving a shop. Which farewell is appropriate (formal)?
exercises.explanation: Shops and strangers run the Sie-line: Auf Wiedersehen. Tschüss is for the du-circle.

exercises.prompt: Complete the informal exchange: 'Wie geht's? — Danke, gut! _____?'
exercises.explanation: The dative return question mirrors the ask: dir after du-address, Ihnen after Sie.

exercises.prompt: Which part of 'Auf Wiedersehen' means SEE?
exercises.explanation: Wieder-sehen = re-see: the farewell literally says 'until [we] see [each other] again' — the same logic as French au revoir.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the German sentence you hear:
exercises.target_answer: Guten Tag wie geht es Ihnen
exercises.meaning: Good day! How goes it to-you-formal?
exercises.explanation: The full formal opener: Guten Tag + the dative question — es geht ES Ihnen (to-you-formal), capital I.
exercises.spoken: Guten Tag wie geht es Ihnen
cues: Meaning: "Good day! How goes it to-you-formal?"
Opens with "Guten Tag" and ends with "Ihnen".

summary.outcome: Run both greeting scripts and switch register without hesitation.

use_example.german: Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen? — Danke, gut!
use_example.english: Good day! How are you? — Thanks, well!

summary.takeaway: Greetings are sentences in costume: good-day, until-re-seeing — and the du/Sie switch decides dir vs Ihnen.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Gift, Rat & Co. — the six highest-value false friends, in the wild.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Greetings & Goodbyes Gym (Good day! How goes it to-you-formal):
twist.target_answer: Guten Tag wie geht es Ihnen
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Guten Tag wie geht es Ihnen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Greetings & Goodbyes Gym without relying on short-term echo.

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

abend.context_phrase: Am Abend lese ich ein Buch.
abend.context_translation: In the evening I read a book.
abend.etymology_derivation: The twin of archaic English even/eve ('evening') — the same *ēbandaz root; Guten Abend keeps the wish-accusative. [wiktionary]

sehen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *sehwaną — the identical twin of see (and gesehen ↔ seen); initial s voiced before vowels. [wiktionary]

neffe.context_phrase: Mein Neffe ist zwei Jahre alt.
neffe.context_translation: My nephew is two years old.
neffe.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nefô; English nephew is a Latin (nepos) loan — the same PIE kinship root. [wiktionary]

schwiegermutter.etymology_derivation: Schwieger (Old High German swigar; no English cognate) + Mutter, the twin of English mother. [wiktionary]

junge.etymology_derivation: Nominalized jung (young), Proto-Germanic *jungaz — the direct cognate of English young. [wiktionary]

trocken.etymology_derivation: Old High German truckan 'dry, parched' — related to English dry. [wiktionary]

löwe.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *lewo; only Dutch leeuw named — no English cognate, memorize this one. [wiktionary]

kohl.etymology_derivation: From Old High German kol, an early borrowing of Latin caulis, meaning stalk or cabbage stem; English kale and cole descend from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

mutig.etymology_derivation: Mut (courage) plus -ig, Proto-Germanic *mōdagaz, whose English twin is moody — in Old English moody still meant brave and only later slid to gloomy. [wiktionary]

träne.context_phrase: Eine Träne läuft ihr über das Gesicht.
träne.context_translation: A tear runs down her face.
träne.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German træne, from Old High German trahan, from Proto-West Germanic *trahnu. English tear is a cognate. [wiktionary]

fischer.context_phrase: Der Fischer fährt früh aufs Meer.
fischer.context_translation: The fisherman goes out to sea early.
fischer.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vischære, from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz - the exact twin of the English surname Fisher (fish + -er). [wiktionary]

garderobe.context_phrase: Die Jacken hängen an der Garderobe.
garderobe.context_translation: The coats hang on the coat rack.
garderobe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French garde-robe, guard-robe — the exact compound of English wardrobe, whose warder is the same Frankish guard-word. [wiktionary][etymonline]
